section.title: The Kings of the North and South
section.sectionRationale: The heart of the final vision is a strikingly detailed prophecy of the wars between the kingdoms that arose from Alexander's empire, the kings of the North and South, converging on a despicable king who desecrates the temple, halts the sacrifice, and persecutes those loyal to God. The wise instruct many and are refined through suffering. The chapter shows God's total command of history's smallest turns, and the certain end of every proud tyrant who exalts himself against Him.
section.thesis: God foretells the tangled wars of the North and South and the rise of a blasphemous king who desecrates the sanctuary and crushes the faithful, yet the vision insists that all runs to God's appointed time, that the wise who know their God will resist and instruct many, and that the self-exalting tyrant will come to his end with no one to help him.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Persia, Greece, and the breakup of Alexander's empire; the long wars of the kings of the South and North; the despicable king who defiles the covenant and the wise who resist; and the king who exalts himself above every god and meets his appointed end.

units.label: Persia, Greece, and Alexander's divided empire
units.note: a kingdom broken to the four winds

verses.text: Now then, I will tell you the truth: Three more kings will arise in Persia, and then a fourth, who will be far richer than all the others. By the power of his wealth, he will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece.
Then a mighty king will arise, who will rule with great authority and do as he pleases.

But as soon as he is established, his kingdom will be broken up and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven. It will not go to his descendants, nor will it have the authority with which he ruled, because his kingdom will be uprooted and given to others.

units.label: The long wars of South and North

verses.text: The king of the South will grow strong, but one of his commanders will grow even stronger and will rule his own kingdom with great authority.

After some years they will form an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the South will go to the king of the North to seal the agreement. But his daughter will not retain her position of power, nor will his strength endure. At that time she will be given up, along with her royal escort and her father and the one who supported her.
But one from her family line will rise up in his place, come against the army of the king of the North, and enter his fortress, fighting and prevailing.
He will take even their gods captive to Egypt, with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold. For some years he will stay away from the king of the North,
who will invade the realm of the king of the South and then return to his own land.
But his sons will stir up strife and assemble a great army, which will advance forcefully, sweeping through like a flood, and will again carry the battle as far as his fortress.
In a rage, the king of the South will march out to fight the king of the North, who will raise a large army, but it will be delivered into the hand of his enemy.
When the army is carried off, the king of the South will be proud in heart and will cast down tens of thousands, but he will not triumph.
For the king of the North will raise another army, larger than the first, and after some years he will advance with a great army and many supplies.
In those times many will rise up against the king of the South. Violent ones among your own people will exalt themselves in fulfillment of the vision, but they will fail.
Then the king of the North will come, build up a siege ramp, and capture a fortified city. The forces of the South will not stand; even their best troops will not be able to resist.
The invader will do as he pleases, and no one will stand against him. He will establish himself in the Beautiful Land, with destruction in his hand.

He will resolve to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and will reach an agreement with the king of the South. He will give him a daughter in marriage in order to overthrow the kingdom, but his plan will not succeed or help him.
Then he will turn his face to the coastlands and capture many of them. But a commander will put an end to his reproach and will turn it back upon him.
After this, he will turn back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be no more.
In his place one will arise who will send out a tax collector for the glory of the kingdom; but within a few days he will be destroyed, though not in anger or in battle.

units.label: The despicable king and the faithful who resist

verses.text: In his place a despicable person will arise; royal honors will not be given to him, but he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingdom by intrigue.
Then a flood of forces will be swept away before him and destroyed, along with a prince of the covenant.
After an alliance is made with him, he will act deceitfully; for he will rise to power with only a few people.

In a time of peace, he will invade the richest provinces and do what his fathers and forefathers never did. He will lavish plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers, and he will plot against the strongholds, but only for a time.
And with a large army he will stir up his power and his courage against the king of the South, who will mobilize a very large and powerful army but will not withstand the plots devised against him.
Those who eat from his provisions will seek to destroy him; his army will be swept away, and many will fall slain.
And the two kings, with their hearts bent on evil, will speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time.
The king of the North will return to his land with great wealth, but his heart will be set against the holy {{berith|covenant}}; so he will do damage and return to his own land.
At the appointed time he will invade the South again, but this time will not be like the first.

Ships of Kittim will come against him, and he will lose heart. Then he will turn back and rage against the holy covenant and do damage. So he will return and show favor to those who forsake the holy covenant.
His forces will rise up and desecrate the temple fortress. They will abolish the daily sacrifice and set up the {{shiqquts|abomination of desolation}}.
With flattery he will corrupt those who violate the covenant, but the people who know their God will firmly resist him.
Those with {{maskilim|insight}} will instruct many, though for a time they will fall by sword or flame, or be captured or plundered.
Now when they fall, they will be granted a little help, but many will join them insincerely.
Some of the wise will fall so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless until the time of the end, for it will still come at the {{moed|appointed time}}.

units.label: The king who exalts himself and his end
units.note: he will come to his end with no one to help

verses.text: Then the king will do as he pleases and will exalt and magnify himself above every god, and he will speak monstrous things against the God of gods. He will be successful until the time of wrath is completed, for what has been decreed must be accomplished.
He will show no regard for the gods of his fathers, nor for the one desired by women, nor for any other god, because he will magnify himself above them all.
And in their place, he will honor a god of fortresses, a god his fathers did not know, with gold, silver, precious stones, and riches.
He will attack the strongest fortresses with the help of a foreign god and will greatly honor those who acknowledge him, making them rulers over many and distributing the land for a price.

At the time of the end, the king of the South will engage him in battle, but the king of the North will storm out against him with chariots, horsemen, and many ships, invading many countries and sweeping through them like a flood.
He will also invade the Beautiful Land, and many countries will fall. But these will be delivered from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the leaders of the Ammonites.
He will extend his power over many countries, and not even the land of Egypt will escape.
He will gain control of the treasures of gold and silver and over all the riches of Egypt, and the Libyans and Cushites will also submit to him.
But news from the east and the north will alarm him, and he will go out with great fury to destroy many and devote them to destruction.
He will pitch his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain, but he will meet his end with no one to help him.

berith.gloss: A covenant, the sacred bond between God and His people. The persecuting king sets his heart against the holy covenant, attacking not just a nation but the covenant relationship with God, and he rewards those who forsake it. The whole conflict is over loyalty to God's covenant.

shiqquts.gloss: The abomination of desolation, a detestable thing that defiles and lays waste. The king's forces halt the daily sacrifice and set up this abomination in the temple. Jesus takes up the very phrase in His teaching about coming judgment, showing the pattern reaches beyond its first fulfillment.

maskilim.gloss: Those who have insight, the wise. In the persecution they instruct many and stand firm, yet some fall and are refined through suffering. The word links to Daniel 12, where the wise shine like the stars; true wisdom is faithfulness to God that teaches others and endures, even to death.

moed.gloss: An appointed time, a set season. Again and again the vision insists that events, even the persecution and the tyrant's fall, will come at the moed, the time God has fixed. Nothing runs past God's schedule; the suffering is bounded, and the end arrives exactly when He has decreed.

basic.context: The angel gives Daniel an astonishingly detailed forecast of the centuries after him: the last Persian kings, the rise of Greece under a mighty king (Alexander), and the breakup of his empire into rival kingdoms, chiefly the king of the South (Egypt) and the king of the North (Syria). Their endless wars converge on a despicable king who defiles the temple, stops the sacrifice, sets up an abomination, and persecutes the faithful. The wise resist and teach others, some dying, and finally the tyrant exalts himself above every god and comes to his end.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter reads like history written in advance, and its precision is why it matters: God knows and governs the smallest turns of politics and war. Interpreters largely agree the earlier verses trace the Greek and Egyptian-Syrian struggles up to Antiochus IV, who persecuted the Jews around 167 BC. Views differ on whether the closing verses stay with Antiochus or shift to a final antichrist. The steady message is that God rules history and every proud tyrant meets his appointed end.
basic.originalLanguages: The tyrant sets himself against the holy berith, the covenant, and sets up the shiqquts, the abomination that desolates. Against him stand the maskilim, the wise who know their God, instructing many and refined through suffering. And repeatedly the vision anchors everything to the moed, the appointed time God has fixed.
basic.typology: The desecration of the temple and the halting of sacrifice, with the abomination of desolation, form a pattern Jesus applies to later judgment, and which points to the ultimate defiler defeated by Christ. The wise who suffer, teach, and are refined foreshadow the faithful witnesses of every age who share in Christ's sufferings.
basic.christ: The self-exalting king who blasphemes the God of gods and defiles the sanctuary is the very type of the antichrist, whom Christ will destroy. Against him, the people who know their God stand firm, a foretaste of the church that holds to Christ. Jesus took the phrase abomination of desolation onto His own lips, tying this chapter to His coming and the end.
basic.god: God is sovereign over history in breathtaking detail, foretelling kings, marriages, betrayals, and battles centuries ahead. He sets the appointed times, permits persecution for a bounded season, uses suffering to refine His people, and brings every arrogant tyrant to his end exactly when He has decreed. Nothing escapes His command.
basic.crossReferences: First and second Maccabees record the persecution under Antiochus. Matthew 24 has Jesus cite the abomination of desolation. And 2 Thessalonians 2 describes the man of lawlessness who exalts himself, destroyed by Christ.
basic.oneStory: History's wars and tyrants are laid out in advance to show that God holds every thread. A blasphemous king will defile what is holy and crush the faithful, but only for an appointed time, and then he will fall with no one to help him. The pattern points to the final enemy and his certain defeat by Christ, and to the wise who, through suffering, hold fast to the God who governs it all.

context.literary:
The chapter is a single speech by the messenger, begun at 10:20 and running without a break to 12:4. Its shape is a funnel. It opens with a wide sweep, four Persian kings and one mighty Greek, verses 2 to 4, narrows to two rival dynasties and their long exchange of blows, verses 5 to 20, and then slows almost to a stop on one man, verses 21 to 35, who receives a third of the whole chapter. The last stage, verses 36 to 45, is a portrait of a king whose pride has no limit and whose end is announced. The farther the speech goes, the more detail it supplies, which is the opposite of what we expect when a writer is remembering the past.

The writer keeps a small set of refrains that tie the verses together. Kings "do as they please," verses 3, 16 and 36, echoing the ram and the goat of 8:4 and 8:8. Nearly every king is given an ally, a daughter, a flood, or a ruse. And again and again the vision stops to say that a thing will happen "at the appointed time," verses 27, 29, 35 and 40, so that the chaos of politics is repeatedly bracketed by a schedule not made by kings.

Three marriages, or attempts at marriages, mark the narrative: the daughter of the South goes north in verse 6, a daughter of the North goes south in verse 17, and the two kings share a table of lies in verse 27. Each is a diplomatic move, and each is shown to fail. The only alliance that stands is the one that cannot be seen, between God and the people who know Him, verse 32.

Within the whole of the book, chapter 11 is the long form of what chapters 2, 7 and 8 gave in outline. Where chapter 8 named the ram and the goat and the little horn, chapter 11 names the days and deals of the kings who followed.
context.historical:
Most of the verses from 2 to 35 can be matched, with remarkable closeness, to the history that followed Daniel. The four kings after Cyrus are usually counted as Cambyses, Bardiya, Darius I and Xerxes, and the "far richer" fourth is generally taken as Xerxes, whose expedition against Greece in 480 BC stirred up the whole Greek world. The "mighty king" of verse 3 is Alexander the Great, who died in 323 BC while still young, and whose realm was split among his generals. Four of those successors, Cassander, Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy, ended up with the main portions.

From there the story is that of two of those dynasties. Ptolemy and his Egyptian line are the kings of the South, and Seleucus and his Syrian line are the kings of the North. The land of Israel lay between them and was fought over for roughly a century and a half. Verse 6 corresponds to the marriage of Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, to Antiochus II, around 250 BC, which ended in murder. Verses 7 to 9 fit the counter-invasion by her brother, Ptolemy III. Verses 10 to 19 describe the career of Antiochus III the Great, who defeated Egypt and took the "Beautiful Land," that is Judea, around 200 BC. He gave a daughter in marriage to the young Egyptian king in verse 17, turned west, was checked by a Roman commander, and died plundering a temple in 187 BC. His successor sent a tax collector, verse 20, and was soon removed, not in open battle.

The "despicable person" of verse 21 is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who took the throne in 175 BC by intrigue, not by right of succession. His two Egyptian campaigns, in 170 and 168 BC, and the humbling at the hands of a Roman envoy, who drew a circle around him in the sand and demanded an answer, match verses 25 to 30. The "ships of Kittim" are Roman ships, and the name is already used in this sense in Numbers 24:24. In December 167 BC Antiochus banned the Jewish rites, stopped the daily sacrifice, and set up a pagan altar in the temple, which the books of the Maccabees describe in detail. The revolt led by the Maccabees is the background of verses 32 to 35.
context.canonical:
The chapter assumes the earlier visions. The four kingdoms of Daniel 2 and 7 and the ram and goat of Daniel 8 are the same story told in different pictures, and chapter 11 supplies the details of the third and fourth stages. The speaker's phrase that these things are written in the Book of Truth, 10:21, is what gives the whole detailed forecast its authority.

The portrait of the persecutor in verses 36 to 39 belongs with a series of arrogant kings in Scripture who speak as if they were gods: Pharaoh in Exodus 5:2, the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14:13 to 14, and the ruler of Tyre in Ezekiel 28:2. Daniel 7:25 has the little horn who speaks against the Most High and wears down the saints, which is the same figure in a different picture.

In the New Testament the figure keeps growing. Paul speaks of the man of lawlessness who exalts himself above every so-called god and seats himself in the temple, 2 Thessalonians 2:3 to 4, and John describes a beast given a mouth to speak great blasphemies, Revelation 13:5 to 6. John even says that "many antichrists" have already appeared, 1 John 2:18, which implies a pattern and not a single event. Jesus takes the "abomination of desolation" from Daniel and warns His disciples about it in Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14, and Luke records the same warning as the sight of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, Luke 21:20.

The faithful who suffer are tied to other texts as well. The "wise" who instruct many in verse 33 echo the Servant in Isaiah 52:13 and 53:11, and the martyrs who refuse release for a better resurrection in Hebrews 11:35 describe the same kind of faithfulness the chapter praises in verses 32 to 35.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The messenger tells Daniel the truth, 11:2, and what this reveals to the first hearers is first of all a claim about God. A people squeezed between two superpowers would have read their own history as chaos, with armies marching over their land every few years. Chapter 11 says that none of it was chaos. Every campaign, wedding and betrayal was known and bounded. That is a message for people who could not change the course of events but needed to know who held them.

It is also a message about how to live under pressure. Verses 32 to 35 are the heart of the chapter, and they turn the reader from watching kings to watching the faithful. When a tyrant uses flattery to corrupt, some will give in. But the people who know their God will be strong and act. The writer wants his readers to be among those, and tells them honestly what it will cost: sword, flame, captivity and plunder. He also tells them that the suffering is purposeful, that it refines, and that it is not unlimited. The tyrant may succeed, but only "until the time of wrath is completed," verse 36.

A final aim is to cultivate patience. The vision states four times that things will happen at the appointed time. The reader is invited to trust the schedule even when the persecution is at its height.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is a long forecast, and a forecast is not a command. It describes the actions of ungodly kings, including their cruelty, deceit and violence, without approving any of them. It would be a serious mistake to read the broken treaties, the lies at the table or the plundering as models to follow. What the text approves is narrow and plain: those who know their God resist, instruct others, and endure.

Equally, the details are not a code for matching today's news. People have tried to find the king of the North in various modern states, and every generation has found its own match. The text does not invite it. Its repeated stress is on the appointed time, which belongs to God, and Jesus said that no one but the Father knows the day and hour, Matthew 24:36. The right application is steadiness, not speculation: stand firm when pressure comes, be willing to teach others the truth, and expect God to deal with tyrants in His time.

The warning also applies to the temptation of those who would use the figure of the persecutor against their rivals. The scriptural use of the pattern is to call the church to faithfulness, not to label opponents.

debates.question: Where does the prophecy move from Antiochus IV to the end of the age?

views.label: It stays with Antiochus throughout
views.case: Verse 36 begins with simply "the king," with no new character announced, and 'in the time of wrath' and 'the king of the South' continue the same wars. On this reading the king who exalts himself is Antiochus, who took the title Epiphanes, 'God manifest,' and who set up the worship of Zeus in the temple. Verses 40 to 45 are either a poetic summary of his last campaigns or a prediction that was not fulfilled as written, since history records that he died in the east, in Persia, around 164 BC.

views.label: A shift at verse 36 to a future figure
views.case: Many conservative interpreters see a change at verse 36. The king there does 'as he pleases' without limit, honors a god his fathers did not know, and rules until the time of wrath is complete, which sounds more like Paul's man of lawlessness than like Antiochus. Verse 40 also says 'at the time of the end,' and 12:1 follows at once with 'at that time,' pointing to the final distress and resurrection. Antiochus's death does not match verses 40 to 45.

views.label: A shift at verse 40 or a blending
views.case: Others see the Antiochus portrait continuing through verse 39 and then merging into the end-time figure, so that the later pattern is anticipated in the earlier. This view has the benefit of taking seriously both the strong fit with Antiochus and the lack of any obvious historical match for verses 40 to 45.

debates.bearing: The language of the text keeps turning between the near and the far, which is one of the ways biblical prophecy works. What matters most is that the pattern is identical whichever figure is meant: a king who exalts himself, persecutes the holy people, and comes to his end with no one to help him, verse 45. The Old Testament gave God's people a type, and the New Testament shows that it recurs.

debates.question: Is this prophecy written in advance, or history written afterwards?

views.label: Prediction from the sixth century BC
views.case: The book presents Daniel as a Babylonian and Persian court figure and says that these things were told to him. Conservative readers note that Jesus speaks of 'Daniel the prophet,' Matthew 24:15, that Ezekiel refers to a righteous Daniel in Ezekiel 14:14, and that the last verses of the chapter do not match the known history of Antiochus, which is odd if the writer had the events in front of him.

views.label: A Maccabean-era author writing as history after the fact
views.case: Many critical scholars date the book to about 165 BC. They point out that the detail of the chapter is dense and accurate down to the death of Antiochus's predecessors and then becomes vague and wrong, which they take to mark the point at which the author passed from known events to hopeful predictions. They also note that Daniel appears among the Writings in the Hebrew canon and treat the language and setting as later.

debates.bearing: The question cannot be settled by the content of the chapter alone, and it should be approached with honesty. What is common to both sides is that the chapter proclaims a God who rules history and who will deliver the faithful. The church has also received the book as Scripture on the authority of Christ, who treats Daniel as a prophet.

study.originalLanguages:
The vocabulary of verses 21 to 35 rewards slow reading, because the writer chooses words that echo other parts of Scripture. The "despicable person" of verse 21 is nivzeh, a passive participle of the root that means to despise. Isaiah 53:3 uses the same form for the Servant, who was "despised and rejected." The tyrant is a despised man who seizes honor, and the true king is a despised man who is given it. The contrast is not announced, but a careful reader hears it.

The tyrant takes power "by intrigue," a word, chalaqlaqqot, from the root for smoothness, which means that he moves by flattery and slippery talk. A related word returns in verse 32, where he "corrupts" the covenant breakers "with flattery." The text has already told us that his strength is not primarily force but persuasion, and that persuasion works only on those who have already loosened their grip on the covenant.

Verse 31 speaks of the "daily sacrifice," ha-tamid, the continual offering of morning and evening, Exodus 29:38 to 42. The word tamid means "continual" and in Daniel 8:11 to 13 and 12:11 it is what the desolator takes away. The sanctuary is the "temple fortress," a phrase that joins the idea of holiness with the idea of defense, and the fact that it can be desecrated shows that no earthly stronghold is secure. The forces who do it "rise up," literally their arms stand, and this is a standing army pitched against a holy place.

Verse 32 has a short, strong sentence: the people who know their God yachaziqu ve'asu, "will be strong and act." The verb chazaq, to be strong, is the same one repeated at 10:19. Strength has just been given to Daniel, and now it is expected of the people. Knowledge of God is the root of courage. Verse 33 adds that the wise will "instruct many," a phrase that Isaiah 53:11 uses of the Servant making many righteous. Verse 35 says some of the wise will fall in order "to be refined," from the root tsaraf, used of the smelting of silver, Zechariah 13:9, and Malachi 3:3.

The verb in verse 36 behind "what has been decreed," nechertsah, comes from charats, to decide or cut. The same root appears in Daniel 9:26 and 9:27 for the desolations "decreed" and the end "decreed" to be poured out. The vision of chapter 11 is the working out of the decree announced in chapter 9. The "time of wrath," zaam, is the period of indignation, a word that is also used for God's anger at His people in Isaiah 10:5 and 10:25.

The "Beautiful Land" is ha-tsevi, from the word for beauty or splendor, used of the land in 8:9, and of the holy mountain in verse 45. The speaker names Israel by her glory, even while armies cross it. And the strange phrase in verse 37, "the one desired by women," uses the root chamad, desire, which was also behind Daniel's title in 10:11. Whether it names a pagan deity, as many suppose, or something else, is uncertain, and the text does not tell us.

typology.type: Antiochus IV as a pattern of the final persecutor, Daniel 11:21-39
typology.fulfillment: The king who exalts himself above every god, abolishes the true worship and persecutes the faithful becomes the template for later opposition. Paul's man of lawlessness who seats himself in the temple, 2 Thessalonians 2:3 to 4, and John's beast who blasphemes and makes war on the saints, Revelation 13:5 to 7, are drawn with the same strokes. The Lord Jesus will destroy such a figure with the breath of His mouth, 2 Thessalonians 2:8. The type falls short because Antiochus was defeated and died, while the final figure is destroyed in a decisive judgment, Revelation 19:19 to 20.

The desecration of the temple in 167 BC is the first fulfilment of a pattern that Jesus applies to a later event: when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place, flee, Matthew 24:15 to 16. Luke explains it in terms of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, Luke 21:20, which fits the Roman siege of AD 70, and the language of Paul and John suggests a further horizon. Christ is the one who cleanses the temple, John 2:14 to 17, and who describes Himself as the temple, John 2:19. The type falls short because Antiochus defiled a building, while the true desecration the gospel meets is the rejection of the Son.

typology.type: The wise who instruct many and are refined, Daniel 11:33-35
typology.fulfillment: The wise are the faithful who stand firm and teach others, and some are killed for it. They correspond to the Servant of Isaiah, who 'prospers,' from the same root as 'wise,' Isaiah 52:13, and who makes many righteous, Isaiah 53:11. Christ is the true Wise Servant, whose suffering is the means by which many are made righteous. His followers are told to expect similar treatment, John 15:20, and the martyrs of Hebrews 11:35 to 38, who refused release for a better resurrection, are in their line. The type falls short because the wise are refined by their suffering, while the Servant's suffering is not for His own refining but for others.

typology.type: The little help in the time of fall, Daniel 11:34
typology.fulfillment: When the faithful fall, a 'little help' comes, and many join them insincerely. Many identify the help with the Maccabean revolt, and the insincere joiners with the opportunists who followed its success. The pattern is that deliverance in this age is partial and mixed. It prepares the reader for the larger deliverance that comes through resurrection, which is the subject of the next chapter and of 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23. The type falls short because every earthly rescue, even a good one, is incomplete and compromised, while the rescue in Christ is complete.

study.christ:
This chapter does not mention a Savior by name or office, and the right way to approach it is by contrast. The chapter's main figure is a king who exalts and magnifies himself, verse 36. The gospel's main figure is the One who, though in the form of God, emptied Himself and took the form of a servant, and whom God therefore highly exalted, Philippians 2:5 to 11. The tyrant is despised, takes honor by flattery, and goes down with no helper, verse 45. The Servant is despised, refuses to take honor for Himself, and is raised up by God, Isaiah 52:13 and 53:3. Jesus Himself taught the principle that everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, Luke 14:11, and the two paths in this chapter and in the gospel are examples of it.

Second, Jesus takes up Daniel's phrase. The abomination of desolation, which was a historical atrocity under Antiochus, becomes in His teaching a warning for His own generation and a sign of the end, Matthew 24:15. He also lays down the same pattern of endurance that this chapter describes. He tells His disciples that they will be handed over, hated and killed, and that the one who endures to the end will be saved, Matthew 24:9 to 13. The call of the maskilim to be strong and act is renewed in Him, and with a better promise: He says that He has overcome the world, John 16:33.

Third, the people who "know their God" in verse 32 find their fullest definition in Jesus, who prays that eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent, John 17:3. Knowing God here is not an abstract matter, and the people of the Messiah are the ones who know Him in the person of the Son.

Fourth, the end of the persecutor. The man of lawlessness will be destroyed by the Lord Jesus with the breath of His mouth, 2 Thessalonians 2:8, and the beast and its armies are defeated by the rider whose name is King of kings and Lord of lords, Revelation 19:16 to 21. The tyrant in this chapter speaks against the God of gods; the Lord who comes is the One to whom every knee bows.

The chapter should not be allegorized. Antiochus is Antiochus, and the Egyptian and Syrian kings were real. But the pattern of the chapter is intended to lead to Christ, who is both the contrast to the proud and the One who will defeat them.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter says about God is by omission. Its verbs are the verbs of kings: they rise, march, marry, deceive and plunder. God is rarely named, and only as "their God" and the "God of gods." Yet it is clear that the events are His. He is the one who writes the schedule, who sets the limits, and who knows the end. A reader who looks for God in the text will find Him in the margins, as in the book of Esther, and will learn that hiddenness is not absence.

Second, it shows a God whose knowledge of history is complete and detailed. Isaiah says that He declares the end from the beginning, Isaiah 46:9 and 10, and that is not only true of the great sweep but of the small turns: a marriage, a tax collector, a Roman envoy. Nothing in the political world slips beyond Him. That knowledge is not a bare fact; it is the basis on which the faithful are told to stand firm.

Third, the chapter holds together two things that are often thought to conflict. The kings act freely and are blamed for their pride, deceit and cruelty. Their "hearts are bent on evil," verse 27. And yet their success is limited by what God has decreed: it lasts "only for a time," verse 24, and "until the time of wrath is completed," verse 36. The Bible does not explain how both are true, but it consistently teaches both, as in Genesis 50:20 and Acts 2:23. God is not the author of the tyrant's sin, but He is the ruler of the tyrant's season.

Fourth, God uses suffering for a purpose. The wise fall "so that they may be refined, purified, and made spotless," verse 35. The persecution is real, and the text does not minimize the sword and the flame. But the same fire that threatens the faithful purifies them, as Peter later writes, 1 Peter 1:6 to 7. God does not cause pain for its own sake, but He is not defeated by it.

For worship, the response is trust and holy fear. The God who is called "God of gods" cannot be matched by any king, and the people who know Him are given the strength to stand. The chapter teaches the church to praise a Lord whose timetable is not changed by the noise of kings.

crossReferences.note: The goat with a prominent horn, its broken horn replaced by four, and the little horn who grows toward the Beautiful Land and takes away the daily sacrifice. Chapter 11 supplies the names and dealings behind these animals, and shows they are about the same course of events.

The small horn speaks against the Most High, wears down the saints and tries to change times and laws, for a time, times and half a time. This is the same persecutor as the king of Daniel 11:36, seen in the language of Daniel's own dream.

Balaam foretells ships from the coasts of Cyprus that will subdue Asshur and Eber. The name Kittim is used in this way for a western naval power, which supports the view that the ships of Kittim in Daniel 11:30 are those of Rome.

The king of Babylon says in his heart that he will ascend to heaven and make himself like the Most High. It is the classic portrait of the ruler who exalts himself above God, and Daniel 11:36 draws the same character in a later king.

By his knowledge the righteous Servant makes many righteous. The wise who instruct many in Daniel 11:33 share the Servant's task and the Servant's suffering, and the link ties the faithful minority of the chapter to the Servant they imitate.

Jesus places the abomination of desolation in the future of His own hearers and links it with the greatest distress. He treats Daniel 11:31 as a pattern that is still unfolding, and tells believers how to respond: flee, endure and trust the God who shortens the days.

Paul describes the man of lawlessness who exalts himself above every so-called god and takes his seat in God's temple, and whom the Lord Jesus will destroy by the breath of His mouth. The pattern of Daniel 11:36 to 45 is taken up and given its final end.

The beast is given a mouth to utter proud words and blasphemies for forty-two months, and is allowed to make war on the saints. The words and the limit in time echo Daniel 11:36 and 7:25, and show the same persecutor in the last act.

Some were tortured and refused release so that they might gain a better resurrection, and others were stoned, sawn in two and killed with the sword. It describes the cost named in Daniel 11:33 and puts the sufferers among the heroes of faith.

Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God, humbled Himself to death on a cross, and God highly exalted Him. It is the perfect contrast with the king of Daniel 11:36, who magnifies himself and falls, and shows the real way to glory.
God declares the end from the beginning and says His purpose will stand. The detailed forecast of Daniel 11 is an example of what He claims here, and gives the reason that He alone is God.

God will bring a remnant through the fire, refine them like silver and test them like gold, and they will call on His name. It supplies the picture behind Daniel 11:35, where the suffering of the wise is a refining.

study.oneStory:
From the earliest pages, the Bible has two kinds of kingdoms in view. There are the kingdoms that seek to make a name for themselves, from Babel in Genesis 11 to Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar and Alexander, and there is the kingdom of the God who made the world and chose a people to carry His promise. Daniel 11 is a long, dark chapter in the history of the first kind of kingdom, and it shows how they behave when they meet the second.

The chapter answers a question that the exile had left open. If God is king, why do foreign powers keep walking across His land? The answer is that He knows each of them, limits each of them, and uses them. It also shows that the real struggle is between those who exalt themselves and those who know their God. Persecution and faithfulness are old themes: Cain and Abel, Joseph's brothers, Pharaoh and the midwives, Haman and Mordecai. Here they are set in a particular age, under Antiochus, and given a face.

It sets up what comes next. The terrible king dies without a helper, and the next verse, 12:1, introduces the time of unmatched distress, the rising of Michael and the deliverance of those written in the book. The pattern of this chapter will recur: with the Roman siege of Jerusalem, with the persecutions of the early church, and finally with the last great rebellion. At each stage the same question is asked, and the same answer is given.

The story ends in the new creation, where there are no more kings of the North and South and no more flattery that corrupts. The nations are healed, and the one who is called King of kings reigns, Revelation 19:16 and 22:2. The people who endured under pressure are named as those who overcame by the blood of the Lamb, Revelation 12:11. The wise who taught many and fell by the sword will be told, as the next chapter says, that they will shine like the stars.

quiz.q: What does the mighty king whose empire is broken to the four winds represent?

options.text: The Greek king Alexander, whose vast empire was divided after him and did not pass to his descendants.
options.note: Daniel 11:3-4 matches Alexander and the division of his empire.

options.text: A future Roman emperor.
options.note: The details fit the Greek king Alexander, not a Roman emperor.

options.text: King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon.
options.note: Babylon has already fallen; this is the Greek kingdom.

options.text: King David of Israel.
options.note: This concerns a Gentile empire divided to the four winds, not David.

quiz.q: What was the great offense of the despicable king against God's people?

options.text: He set himself against the holy covenant, halted the daily sacrifice, and set up the abomination of desolation.
options.note: Daniel 11:28-31 centers his crime on defiling the covenant and temple.

options.text: He merely raised taxes on the people.
options.note: Taxation appears earlier of another king; his defining sin was defiling the covenant and sanctuary.

options.text: He rebuilt the temple grander than before.
options.note: The opposite; he desecrated the temple and stopped the sacrifice.

options.text: He freed the Jewish people from oppression.
options.note: He persecuted them and defiled their worship.

quiz.q: How do the people who know their God respond in the persecution?

options.text: They firmly resist him, and the wise instruct many, though some fall and are refined through suffering.
options.note: Daniel 11:32-35 shows faithful resistance and refining.

options.text: They all abandon their faith to survive.
options.note: Some join insincerely, but the people who know God stand firm.

options.text: They flee and are never heard from again.
options.note: They resist and teach many, even at the cost of their lives.

options.text: They join the king's cause enthusiastically.
options.note: They resist him firmly; it is the covenant violators he corrupts.

quiz.q: What is the repeated assurance about the timing of these events?

options.text: Everything comes at the appointed time God has fixed, and the end will still come as decreed.
options.note: Daniel 11:27, 29, 35 anchor events to God's appointed time.

options.text: The events happen randomly and cannot be predicted.
options.note: The opposite; the vision stresses God's fixed, appointed times.

options.text: The tyrant sets the timing himself.
options.note: The tyrant prospers only until the time of wrath God has decreed is complete.

options.text: No one, not even God, knows when the end will come.
options.note: The end comes at God's appointed time, already decreed.

quiz.q: How does the self-exalting king point to Christ's victory?

options.text: He is a type of the antichrist who blasphemes God, yet meets his end with no one to help, foreshadowing the final enemy Christ destroys.
options.note: The pattern points to the man of lawlessness destroyed by Christ, 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

options.text: He shows that arrogant kings always win in the end.
options.note: The opposite; he comes to his end with no one to help him.

options.text: He teaches that God cannot stop powerful rulers.
options.note: God brings him to his appointed end; He is fully sovereign.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The blasphemous king prefigures the antichrist whom Christ defeats.

questions: God foretold the wars of kings in astonishing detail. How does His command of history's smallest turns give you confidence in the middle of chaotic world events?
The people who knew their God stood firm when others compromised. What does it look like for you to know God deeply enough to resist pressure?
The wise instructed many even while suffering. Who has God placed around you to teach and strengthen, even at personal cost?
Some of the wise fell in order to be refined and made spotless. How does it reframe your trials to see them as God refining your faith rather than abandoning you?
The proud king prospered only until the appointed time, then fell. How does the certainty that evil has a fixed limit help you endure a season when the wicked seem to win?

translationNotes.note: Greece renders the Hebrew Javan; the mighty king who follows is widely identified with Alexander the Great.
Ships of Kittim refers to western coastlands or Mediterranean islands, historically the intervention of Rome that turned Antiochus back from Egypt.
The abomination of desolation is the phrase Jesus takes up in Matthew 24:15; here it marks the desecration of the temple and halting of the daily sacrifice.
The one desired by women is variously understood; the point is the king's utter contempt for every god and loyalty, magnifying only himself.
